newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian Grain - Soymeal buying picks-up pre-USDA.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Soymeal buying picks-up pre-USDA.

text.p: Southeast Asian buyers are nibbling at the edges of the soymeal market, but are generally waiting for key U.S. crop data due later on Wednesday to determine market direction, regional traders said.
The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) releases its September U.S. crop report at 1230 GMT on Wednesday.
"Everybody's waiting for the report to come out because that will determine buying patterns here over the next few months," one Singapore-based trader said.
But traders said three buyers in Malaysia had recently bought about 30,000 tonnes of Argentine soymeal for September/October delivery at around $295-$305 a tonne C&F.
"That's a deal that was concluded recently," one said.
"I believe that's true," a dealer in a Western commodity company said. "I think it was done late last week."
One trader said he believed the price of the deal was closer to $305 a tonne than $295.
"The lower figure does not fit in well with the current price of soymeal in the market," he said.

Potential buyers in the region are interested in procuring Indian origin soymeal, but supplies will not be available until November when the harvest comes in. There were unconfirmed reports that three Malaysian buyers were in the market for 20,000 tonnes of Indian product.
"There is interest (in Indian soymeal), but they have time to make up their mind so there's no rush," another dealer said.

A senior purchasing official at Ho Seng Chan, one of Malaysia's four largest soymeal buyers, said he could be in the market soon. "I may be buying some soymeal after the U.S. trade report comes out between September 12 and 13," he said.
Imported soymeal prices stabilised in Malaysia this week at around 760 ringgit ($305) a tonne after being quoted at between 760-773 ringgit at the end of August.
In Thailand, the price of locally-crushed soymeal from imported beans rose to 10.05 baht a kg from between 9.70-9.75 baht last week due to tight supply, local traders said.
Domestic soymeal stocks are diminishing as imported soymeal from Brazil for August and September shipment has yet to arrive in Bangkok, they said.
Thai feed millers said they had ordered 50,000 tonnes of low quality soymeal from Brazil at below $300 a tonne C&F Bangkok.
Indonesian soymeal prices were also offered at higher levels this week at between 815-820 rupiah/kg in Jakarta compared with around 790 rupiah/kg last week.
In the regional corn market, Indonesian prices remained weak after an unexpectedly high harvest in the main producing regions in Java and Lampung, local traders said.
High quality full yellow corn with a maximum of 16 percent water content was on offer between 480 to 500 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, they said.
Lower grade corn was traded at 490 rupiah in the capital and at between 455 to 460 rupiah/kg in the south Sumatran region of Lampung, the traders added.
"Prices have remained at the same level since last week due to relatively higher supply in the market," one trader with a listed feedmill firm in Jakarta said.
Prices are expected to stay soft next week as corn coming from the main producing regions in east and central Java is likely to start entering Jakarta in higher volumes, he said

Another trader said that the 35,000 tonnes of corn from Argentina which arrived in the middle of last week, coupled with another 30,000 tonnes expected from the United States next week, are likely to keep Indonesian supplies adequate.
He said there was market talk that some firms were in the market for corn from South Africa, but declined to give details.
In Thailand, domestic prices of maize/corn paid by feed producers continued to firm this week as fresh supplies entering the market were scarce, trade sources said.
The price of 14.50 percent-moisture maize was quoted at 4.28-4.40 baht (US 17.0 cents) a kg, compared with 4.16-4.25 baht a kg a week ago, traders said.
They attributed the rise in prices to moonsoon rains which had slowed transportation of the produce to Bangkok.
"The rain also dampened the corn, making it not immediately available for the market," said an official from the Thai Maize and Produce Traders Association.
